sections.title: The Methodology of Political Philosophy
sections.description:
As the story goes, political philosophy experienced a rebirth with the publication of John Rawls’s A Theory of Justice. But after decades of working under the methodological paradigm presupposed in that work, political philosophers and theorists have started to become more reflective about what they are supposed to be doing and how they are supposed to be doing it. As a result, considerable effort has been devoted in the new millennium to debates concerning the relative merits of “ideal” vs. “nonideal” theory, “political moralism” vs. “political realism,” “practice-dependent” vs. “practice-independent” theorizing, and so on. Even political philosophers not directly involved in these debates are increasingly expected to justify their theoretical choices in terms set by them.
This seminar will be a survey of these contemporary methodological debates. It will be organized around three clusters of questions that will help us disentangle what is at stake in them:
(1) At the most general level, we will be asking what the proper aims of political philosophy are. Some hold that its primary or ultimate aim should be to achieve knowledge about political concepts, principles, or ideals. Others hold that its primary or ultimate aim should be to guide the actions of political actors. What would count as an adequate defense of either of these positions? Furthermore, are these our only options? Are there other possible aims, and if so, what are they, and how might they be related to the more familiar ones?
(2) Regardless of the view they take with regards to (1), most political philosophers think that part of what they are supposed to do is identify fundamental ideals or principles that bear on political life. One question we will take up in this regard is whether such ideals or principles depend on facts or not. The answer to this metanormative question is related to more obviously methodological ones concerning, e.g., the extent to which political philosophy can be conducted independently of input from, and dialogue with, related disciplines in the social sciences. A related question here concerns the nature of political ideals or principles: Is there something distinctively political about them, or are they the same as moral ideals and principles? As some put it, is political philosophy just “applied ethics”?
(3) A common and increasingly popular answer to the general question in (1) is that political philosophy should aim, in the first instance, to guide action. If that is the case, then political philosophers must answer a number of related questions. One of them concerns the fruitfulness of “idealization” in the construction of normative political theories. Another concerns the role feasibility judgments ought to play in the justification of action-guiding prescriptions. A further one concerns background theories of political agency: If the aim is to guide action, then presumably philosophers have an agent or group of agents in view whose action is to be guided, and presuppose some account of how their agency is to be effective.
Note. The seminar is intended primarily (though not exclusively) for students with interest and some background in political philosophy or normative political theory, though many of the questions we will take up bear more broadly on what is sometimes called ‘practical philosophy’ and, therefore, on normative ethics as well.
